sentences.text: Shuangbaisaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that may be a junior synonym of Sinosaurus.
This animal possessed a robust skull measuring 54 centimeters in length.
The skull crests were likely formed mainly from the frontal bone, possibly including the postorbital and prefrontal bones.
A groove separating the premaxilla and maxilla at the jaw tip is a defining characteristic, though this feature was previously considered distinctive of Sinosaurus.
Like the contemporary theropods Dilophosaurus and Sinosaurus, Shuangbaisaurus possessed a pair of thin crests in the middle of its skull.
It stands as the third large theropod known to possess a pair of crests on its skull.
Its skull measured 54 centimeters in length with a length-to-height ratio of 2.84, excluding the crests.
The fossil is known from a single partial skull specimen missing most of the snout, stored at the Chuxiong Prefectural Museum.
Remains were discovered in purple muddy siltstone in Liuna Village, Anlongbao Town, Shuangbai County, approximately 100 km south of the Lufeng deposits.
Shuangbaisaurus anlongbaoensis was formally described and named in 2017 by Wang Guo-Fu, You Hai-Lu, Pan Shi-Gang, and Wang Tao.

Alongside Shuangbaisaurus, various dinosaurs from the Fengjiahe Formation have been found, including sauropodomorphs such as Chinshakiangosaurus chunghoensis, Lufengosaurus sp., Yimenosaurus youngi, and Yunnanosaurus huangi.

A diverse fauna represented by trackways has been found in the Fengjiahe Formation deposits, including ichnotaxa such as Eubrontes platypus, Grallator limnosus, Paracoelurosaurichnus monax, Schizograllator xiaohebaensis, Youngichnus xiyangensis, and Zhengichnus jinningensis.
Shuangbaisaurus belongs to the order Saurischia and the suborder Theropoda.
The vertical groove between the premaxilla and maxilla complicates Shuangbaisaurus classification, as it was previously considered a distinguishing feature of Sinosaurus.
Shuangbaisaurus lived in the Early Jurassic of Yunnan Province, China, specifically during the Hettangian stage from 201.4 to 199.5 million years ago.
In 2019, Philip Currie and colleagues suggested that the Shuangbaisaurus specimen might fall within the variation of Sinosaurus triassicus.
